title: Die beiden Wanderer
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 107. Text from Wikisource („Die beiden Wanderer (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 107 pairs a good-natured tailor with a shoemaker whose envy of him curdles into real cruelty. Lost together in a forest on the longer of two paths, the shoemaker trades his own spare bread for the tailor's eyes, one and then the other, and abandons him blind beside a gallows. Dew shaken down from the hanged men restores his sight — the tale states the cure as simple fact — and the tailor goes on to a royal court, where ants, ducks and bees repay old kindnesses by completing three impossible tasks, and an obliging stork delivers the king a longed-for heir, winning the tailor a princess in the bargain. The shoemaker, ordered to make the wedding shoes and then banished from the city, ends up back under the very same gallows, where the same crows that once fed on the hanged men peck out his eyes in turn — a tidy, unstated justice the tale leaves entirely to speak for itself.

sentences.t: Berg und Thal begegnen sich nicht, wohl aber die Menschenkinder, zumal gute und böse.
sentences.l: Mountain and valley do not meet one another, but the children of men do, especially good ones and bad.
sentences.i: Mountain and valley never meet, but the children of men do, and good and bad above all.
sentences.n: The tale opens on a proverb. sich begegnen is reciprocal, “to meet one another,” and Menschenkinder — literally “children of men” — is the elevated word for human beings. Thal is the 1857 spelling of Tal.

sentences.t: So kam auch einmal ein Schuster und ein Schneider auf der Wanderschaft zusammen.
sentences.l: So there came once too a cobbler and a tailor together on the journeyman’s road.
sentences.i: And so it came about once that a cobbler and a tailor fell in with each other on their travels.
sentences.n: zusammenkommen is separable and its particle waits at the end: kamen … zusammen. die Wanderschaft is the years of tramping from town to town that a journeyman craftsman was expected to spend before he could settle.

sentences.t: Der Schneider war ein kleiner hübscher Kerl und war immer lustig und guter Dinge.
sentences.l: The tailor was a small handsome fellow and was always merry and of good cheer.
sentences.i: The tailor was a small, good-looking fellow, always merry and in good spirits.
sentences.n: guter Dinge sein is a fixed phrase with a genitive plural — literally “to be of good things” — meaning to be in high spirits.

sentences.t: Er sah den Schuster von der andern Seite heran kommen, und da er an seinem Felleisen merkte was er für ein Handwerk trieb, rief er ihm ein Spottliedchen zu,
sentences.l: He saw the cobbler coming up from the other side, and since he noticed by his pack what trade he plied, he called a little mocking-song out to him,
sentences.i: He saw the cobbler coming toward him from the other side, and since he could tell from his pack what trade the man followed, he called a mocking little song after him:
sentences.n: zurufen is separable — rief … zu, “called out to.” ein Handwerk treiben is “to ply a trade.” Das Felleisen is a leather travelling pack; the unit ends on a comma because the song itself follows.

sentences.t:
„nähe mir die Naht,
ziehe mir den Draht,
streich ihn rechts und links mit Pech,
schlag, schlag mir fest den Zweck.“
sentences.l:
“sew me the seam,
pull me the thread,
stroke it right and left with pitch,
strike, strike the peg in tight for me.”
sentences.i:
“stitch the seam for me,
draw the thread through for me,
rub it right and left with pitch,
hammer, hammer the peg home for me.”
sentences.n: The tailor sings the cobbler’s own work back at him. Naht, Draht, Pech and Zweck are all shoemaker’s things: the seam, the waxed thread, the pitch it is drawn through, and the wooden peg driven in to fasten the sole — der Zweck in this old sense, not the modern “purpose.” The mir in every line is the dative of interest, “for me,” which is the jeer: do my work. The German rhymes; Lectorium’s idiomatic line does not.

sentences.t: Der Schuster aber konnte keinen Spaß vertragen, er verzog ein Gesicht, als wenn er Essig getrunken hätte, und machte Miene das Schneiderlein am Kragen zu packen.
sentences.l: The cobbler, however, could bear no joke, he pulled a face as if he had drunk vinegar, and made as though to seize the little tailor by the collar.
sentences.i: The cobbler, though, could not take a joke; he screwed up his face as if he had drunk vinegar, and made as if to grab the little tailor by the collar.
sentences.n: keinen Spaß vertragen is “to be unable to take a joke.” Miene machen zu is “to make as if to do something.” als wenn takes the past subjunctive hätte, which marks the comparison as unreal.

sentences.t: Der kleine Kerl fieng aber an zu lachen, reichte ihm seine Flasche und sprach „es ist nicht bös gemeint, trink einmal und schluck die Galle hinunter.“
sentences.l: The little fellow, however, began to laugh, handed him his bottle and said “it is not meant badly, drink once and swallow the bile down.”
sentences.i: But the little fellow began to laugh, held out his bottle to him and said, “No harm is meant by it — take a drink and swallow your bile.”
sentences.n: fieng an is the 1857 spelling of fing an, from anfangen, separable. die Galle hinunterschlucken is to swallow one’s gall: the bile was held to be the seat of bad temper.

sentences.t: Der Schuster that einen gewaltigen Schluck, und das Gewitter auf seinem Gesicht fieng an sich zu verziehen.
sentences.l: The cobbler did a mighty gulp, and the thunderstorm on his face began to draw off.
sentences.i: The cobbler took a mighty pull, and the storm on his face began to clear.
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat, from thun (modern tun). sich verziehen is what weather does when it draws away — and it is the same verb used of his face a moment ago, verzog ein Gesicht.

sentences.t: Er gab dem Schneider die Flasche zurück und sprach „ich habe ihr ordentlich zugesprochen, man sagt wohl vom vielen Trinken aber nicht vom großen Durst.
sentences.l: He gave the bottle back to the tailor and said “I have addressed it properly, people speak indeed of the much drinking but not of the great thirst.
sentences.i: He gave the tailor back the bottle and said, “I have done it justice — people talk about heavy drinking, but never about the great thirst behind it.
sentences.n: einer Sache zusprechen, with the dative ihr standing for the bottle, is to help oneself freely to it. wohl … aber concedes before it objects; the cobbler is excusing the length of his pull.

sentences.t: Wollen wir zusammen wandern?“
sentences.l: Shall we wander together?”
sentences.i: Shall we travel on together?”
sentences.n: wollen wir …? is the ordinary German way of proposing something — “shall we,” not “do we want to.”

sentences.t: „Mir ists recht,“ antwortete der Schneider, „wenn du nur Lust hast in eine große Stadt zu gehen, wo es nicht an Arbeit fehlt.“
sentences.l: “It is right by me,” answered the tailor, “if only you have a mind to go into a great city where there is no lack of work.”
sentences.i: “That suits me,” answered the tailor, “provided you have a mind to make for a big city, where work is not wanting.”
sentences.n: ists is ist es run together, and the dative mir gives “it is all right by me.” es fehlt an with the dative is the impersonal “there is a lack of.”

sentences.t: „Gerade dahin wollte ich auch,“ antwortete der Schuster, „in einem kleinen Nest ist nichts zu verdienen, und auf dem Lande gehen die Leute lieber barfuß.“
sentences.l: “Just there I wanted to go too,” answered the cobbler, “in a little nest there is nothing to earn, and in the country people go barefoot by preference.”
sentences.i: “That is exactly where I was bound myself,” answered the cobbler; “in a little nest there is nothing to be earned, and out in the country people would rather go barefoot.”
sentences.n: Ein Nest is a dismissive word for a tiny town. lieber is the comparative of gern, “rather, by preference.” No shoes worn means no work for a cobbler.

sentences.t: Sie wanderten also zusammen weiter und setzten immer einen Fuß vor den andern wie die Wiesel im Schnee.
sentences.l: So they wandered on together and always set one foot before the other like the weasels in the snow.
sentences.i: So they travelled on together, always setting one foot before the other like weasels in the snow.
sentences.n: weiterwandern is separable: wanderten … weiter. The comparison is to the weasel’s track, where each print falls neatly in front of the last.

sentences.t: Zeit genug hatten sie beide, aber wenig zu beißen und zu brechen.
sentences.l: Time enough the two of them had, but little to bite and to break.
sentences.i: Time the two of them had in plenty, but little to bite on and little to break.
sentences.n: The object Zeit genug stands first for emphasis, which puts the verb second and the subject after it. zu beißen und zu brechen is an old pairing for something to eat; brechen here is the breaking of bread.

sentences.t: Wenn sie in eine Stadt kamen, so giengen sie umher und grüßten das Handwerk, und weil das Schneiderlein so frisch und munter aussah und so hübsche rothe Backen hatte, so gab ihm jeder gerne, und wenn das Glück gut war, so gab ihm die Meistertochter unter der Hausthüre auch noch einen Kuß auf den Weg.
sentences.l: When they came into a town, they went about and greeted the trade, and because the little tailor looked so fresh and lively and had such pretty red cheeks, everyone gave to him gladly, and when the luck was good, the master’s daughter under the house door gave him a kiss for the road besides.
sentences.i: When they came to a town they went round greeting the trade, and because the little tailor looked so fresh and lively and had such pretty red cheeks, everyone gave to him readily; and when luck was with him, the master’s daughter in the doorway gave him a kiss for the road into the bargain.
sentences.n: das Handwerk grüßen is the technical phrase for a travelling journeyman presenting himself at the workshops of his craft to ask for work or a gift. The so that opens each main clause simply resumes the sentence after the subordinate one and is not translated. rothe and Hausthüre are the 1857 spellings of rote and Haustüre.

sentences.t: Wenn er mit dem Schuster wieder zusammen traf, so hatte er immer mehr in seinem Bündel.
sentences.l: When he met together with the cobbler again, he always had more in his bundle.
sentences.i: Whenever he fell in with the cobbler again, he always had more in his bundle.
sentences.n: zusammentreffen is separable: traf … zusammen. wenn with a past tense is repeated habit, “whenever.”

sentences.t: Der griesgrämige Schuster schnitt ein schiefes Gesicht und meinte „je größer der Schelm, je größer das Glück.“
sentences.l: The surly cobbler cut a crooked face and said “the bigger the rogue, the bigger the luck.”
sentences.i: The surly cobbler pulled a wry face and said, “the greater the rogue, the greater his luck.”
sentences.n: ein schiefes Gesicht schneiden — to cut a crooked face — is to look sour. je … je is the older form of today’s je … desto, “the more … the more.”

sentences.t: Aber der Schneider fieng an zu lachen und zu singen, und theilte alles, was er bekam, mit seinem Kameraden.
sentences.l: But the tailor began to laugh and to sing, and shared everything that he got with his comrade.
sentences.n: theilte is the 1857 spelling of teilte. This is the detail the whole tale turns on, and the tailor reminds the cobbler of it later, in the forest.

sentences.t: Klingelten nun ein paar Groschen in seiner Tasche, so ließ er auftragen, schlug vor Freude auf den Tisch daß die Gläser tanzten, und es hieß bei ihm „leicht verdient und leicht verthan“.
sentences.l: Did a couple of groschen jingle in his pocket, then he had food brought up, struck the table for joy so that the glasses danced, and with him the word was “lightly earned and lightly spent”.
sentences.i: If a few groschen happened to jingle in his pocket, he would order a meal and thump the table for joy till the glasses danced, and his motto was, “easily earned, easily gone.”
sentences.n: A verb-first clause with no wenn is a conditional: Klingelten nun …, so …, “if a few groschen jingled.” auftragen lassen is to have the dishes brought to the table. Ein Groschen is a small coin; verthan is the 1857 spelling of vertan, from vertun, to squander.

sentences.t: Als sie eine Zeitlang gewandert waren, kamen sie an einen großen Wald, durch welchen der Weg nach der Königsstadt gieng.
sentences.l: When they had wandered a while, they came to a great forest, through which the way to the king’s city went.
sentences.i: When they had travelled a while they came to a great forest, through which the road to the royal city ran.
sentences.n: gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging. durch welchen is the older relative pronoun, where modern German would more often say durch den.

sentences.t: Es führten aber zwei Fußsteige hindurch, davon war der eine sieben Tage lang, der andere nur zwei Tage, aber niemand von ihnen wußte, welcher der kürzere Weg war.
sentences.l: There led, however, two footpaths through it, of which the one was seven days long, the other only two days, but nobody of them knew which was the shorter way.
sentences.i: But two footpaths led through it, one of them seven days long, the other only two, and neither of them knew which was the shorter road.
sentences.n: Es führten opens with the placeholder es and puts the real subject, zwei Fußsteige, after the verb — which is why the verb is plural. davon is “of these.” wußte is the 1857 spelling of wusste.

sentences.t: Die zwei Wanderer setzten sich unter einen Eichenbaum und rathschlagten wie sie sich vorsehen und für wie viel Tage sie Brot mitnehmen wollten.
sentences.l: The two wanderers set themselves down under an oak tree and took counsel how they should provide for themselves and for how many days they wanted to take bread with them.
sentences.i: The two travellers sat down under an oak and took counsel how to provide for themselves, and for how many days they should carry bread.
sentences.n: rathschlagen (modern ratschlagen) is to hold counsel, with Rath, “counsel,” sitting inside it. sich vorsehen is to take precautions. mitnehmen stands whole because it is an infinitive at the end of its clause.

sentences.t: Der Schuster sagte „man muß weiter denken als man geht, ich will für sieben Tage Brot mit nehmen.“
sentences.l: The cobbler said “one must think further than one walks, I will take bread with me for seven days.”
sentences.i: The cobbler said, “A man must think further than he walks; I mean to take bread for seven days.”
sentences.n: The 1857 text prints mit nehmen as two words, where modern German writes mitnehmen. man is the general “one, a person,” and the saying reads as the cobbler’s own rather than a proverb in common circulation.

sentences.t: „Was,“ sagte der Schneider, „für sieben Tage Brot auf dem Rücken schleppen wie ein Lastthier und sich nicht umschauen?
sentences.l: “What,” said the tailor, “drag bread for seven days on the back like a beast of burden and not look about oneself?
sentences.i: “What,” said the tailor, “lug seven days’ bread on my back like a pack animal and never look about me?
sentences.n: The bare infinitives schleppen and umschauen with no finite verb make an indignant exclamation, which English can copy. Lastthier is the 1857 spelling of Lasttier.

sentences.t: ich halte mich an Gott und kehre mich an nichts.
sentences.l: I hold myself to God and turn myself at nothing.
sentences.i: I hold to God and trouble myself about nothing.
sentences.n: sich an etwas kehren is to pay heed to something, so sich an nichts kehren is to care about nothing. The two reflexives are set against each other: holding to God, heeding nothing else.

sentences.t: Das Geld, das ich in der Tasche habe, das ist im Sommer so gut als im Winter, aber das Brot wird in der heißen Zeit trocken und obendrein schimmelig.
sentences.l: The money that I have in my pocket, that is as good in summer as in winter, but the bread turns dry in the hot season and mouldy on top of it.
sentences.i: The money I have in my pocket is as good in summer as in winter, but bread turns dry in the hot weather, and mouldy into the bargain.
sentences.n: The subject is named first and then picked up again by das — a resumptive pronoun that spoken German uses constantly and English drops. so gut als is the older comparison, where modern German has so gut wie.

sentences.t: Mein Rock geht auch nicht länger als auf die Knöchel.
sentences.l: My coat too goes no longer than to the ankles.
sentences.i: My coat too reaches no further than my ankles.
sentences.n: A saying: I do not stretch myself beyond what I have. Knöchel can be either ankle or knuckle, and the coat’s length settles it here.

sentences.t: Warum sollen wir den richtigen Weg nicht finden?
sentences.l: Why should we not find the right way?
sentences.n: sollen here is not obligation but likelihood — “why should we not.”

sentences.t: Für zwei Tage Brot und damit gut.“
sentences.l: Bread for two days and good with that.”
sentences.i: Bread for two days, and let that be enough.”
sentences.n: damit gut is an elliptical dismissal with no verb at all — “and that settles it”; English has to supply one.

sentences.t: Es kaufte sich also ein jeder sein Brot, und dann giengen sie auf gut Glück in den Wald hinein.
sentences.l: So each one bought himself his bread, and then they went into the forest on good luck.
sentences.i: So each of them bought his own bread, and then they walked into the forest and trusted to luck.
sentences.n: auf gut Glück is “at random, trusting to luck.” The dative sich is the reflexive of advantage, “bought for himself.” hineingehen is separable: giengen … hinein.

sentences.t: In dem Wald war es so still wie in einer Kirche.
sentences.l: In the forest it was as still as in a church.
sentences.n: The impersonal es carries a state of the surroundings, much as English says “it was quiet in the forest.”

sentences.t: Kein Wind wehte, kein Bach rauschte, kein Vogel sang, und durch die dichtbelaubten Äste drang kein Sonnenstrahl.
sentences.l: No wind blew, no brook murmured, no bird sang, and through the thickly-leaved branches penetrated no sunbeam.
sentences.i: No wind blew, no brook murmured, no bird sang, and not a ray of sun came through the thick-leaved branches.
sentences.n: The last clause puts its adverbial phrase first, so the verb drang comes before its subject kein Sonnenstrahl — ordinary German order that English cannot copy. dichtbelaubt is a compound of dicht, thick, and belaubt, in leaf.

sentences.t: Der Schuster sprach kein Wort, ihn drückte das schwere Brot auf dem Rücken, daß ihm der Schweiß über sein verdrießliches und finsteres Gesicht herabfloß.
sentences.l: The cobbler spoke not a word, the heavy bread on his back pressed him, so that the sweat flowed down over his sullen and gloomy face.
sentences.i: The cobbler did not speak a word; the heavy bread on his back weighed him down, so that the sweat ran down over his sullen, gloomy face.
sentences.n: ihn drückte das Brot puts the object first: the bread is the subject and he is the one pressed. daß here is “so that,” a result; the dative ihm is where English puts “his.”

sentences.t: Der Schneider aber war ganz munter, sprang daher, pfiff auf einem Blatt oder sang ein Liedchen, und dachte „Gott im Himmel muß sich freuen daß ich so lustig bin.“
sentences.l: The tailor, however, was quite lively, sprang along, whistled on a leaf or sang a little song, and thought “God in heaven must be glad that I am so merry.”
sentences.i: The tailor, though, was thoroughly lively; he came springing along, whistled on a leaf or sang a little song, and thought, “God in heaven must be pleased that I am so merry.”
sentences.n: daherspringen is separable: sprang daher, “came springing along.” muß here is inference, “must surely be,” not compulsion. Whistling on a blade of leaf held between the thumbs is the countryman’s free music.

sentences.t: Zwei Tage gieng das so fort, aber als am dritten Tag der Wald kein Ende nehmen wollte, und der Schneider sein Brot aufgegessen hatte, so fiel ihm das Herz doch eine Elle tiefer herab:
sentences.l: Two days it went on so, but when on the third day the forest would take no end, and the tailor had eaten up his bread, his heart did sink an ell lower:
sentences.i: For two days it went on so, but when on the third day the forest would come to no end, and the tailor had eaten his bread up, his heart did sink a good ell lower.
sentences.n: kein Ende nehmen wollen — wollen of a thing means it refuses to, not that it wants to. An Elle is the old cloth-measure of about two feet, the tailor’s own unit, and here it measures his sinking heart. aufessen is separable.

sentences.t: indessen verlor er nicht den Muth, sondern verließ sich auf Gott und auf sein Glück.
sentences.l: meanwhile he did not lose his courage, but relied on God and on his luck.
sentences.i: Even so, he did not lose heart, but relied on God and on his luck.
sentences.n: indessen here is “nevertheless,” not “meanwhile.” sich verlassen auf is to rely on, quite separate from verlassen, to leave. Muth is the 1857 spelling of Mut.

sentences.t: Den dritten Tag legte er sich Abends hungrig unter einen Baum und stieg den andern Morgen hungrig wieder auf.
sentences.l: The third day he laid himself down hungry in the evening under a tree and got up again hungry the next morning.
sentences.i: On the third day he lay down hungry under a tree in the evening, and got up again hungry the next morning.
sentences.n: Den dritten Tag is a bare accusative of time with no preposition, “on the third day.” stieg … auf is from aufsteigen, used here simply of getting up; the particle waits at the end.

sentences.t: So gieng es auch den vierten Tag, und wenn der Schuster sich auf einen umgestürzten Baum setzte, und seine Mahlzeit verzehrte, so blieb dem Schneider nichts als das Zusehen.
sentences.l: So it went on the fourth day too, and when the cobbler set himself on a fallen tree and consumed his meal, nothing remained to the tailor but the looking on.
sentences.i: So it went on the fourth day too, and whenever the cobbler sat down on a toppled tree and ate his meal, nothing was left to the tailor but to look on.
sentences.n: das Zusehen is an infinitive used as a noun, “the watching.” umgestürzt is the participle of umstürzen, toppled over. The dative dem Schneider marks the man left with nothing.

sentences.t: Bat er um ein Stückchen Brot, so lachte der andere höhnisch und sagte „du bist immer so lustig gewesen, da kannst du auch einmal versuchen wies thut wenn man unlustig ist:
sentences.l: Did he ask for a little piece of bread, then the other laughed scornfully and said “you have always been so merry, so for once you can try how it feels when one is unmerry:
sentences.i: If he asked for a scrap of bread, the other laughed scornfully and said, “You have always been so merry — now you can find out for once how it feels to be unmerry:
sentences.n: Another verb-first conditional without wenn: Bat er …, so …. wies is wie es run together, and wie es einem thut is “how it feels.” unlustig is coined against the tailor’s lustig, so the English keeps the pair.

sentences.t: die Vögel, die Morgens zu früh singen, die stößt Abends der Habicht,“ kurz, er war ohne Barmherzigkeit.
sentences.l: the birds that sing too early in the morning, those the hawk strikes in the evening,” in short, he was without mercy.
sentences.i: the birds that sing too early in the morning are struck by the hawk at evening” — in short, he was without mercy.
sentences.n: A proverb, and the word order is the trap: die Vögel … die is the object and der Habicht the subject, so it is the hawk that does the striking. The resumptive die picks the object up again after the relative clause.

sentences.t: Aber am fünften Morgen konnte der arme Schneider nicht mehr aufstehen und vor Mattigkeit kaum ein Wort herausbringen;
sentences.l: But on the fifth morning the poor tailor could get up no longer and for faintness could scarcely bring out a word;
sentences.i: But on the fifth morning the poor tailor could no longer stand up, and for faintness could hardly bring out a word;
sentences.n: vor with the dative gives the cause of a bodily state, “from faintness.” herausbringen is separable and stands whole here as an infinitive under konnte.

sentences.t: die Backen waren ihm weiß und die Augen roth.
sentences.l: the cheeks were white to him and the eyes red.
sentences.i: his cheeks were white and his eyes red.
sentences.n: The dative of possession: ihm says whose cheeks they are, where English uses “his.” The verb is not repeated in the second half.

sentences.t: Da sagte der Schuster zu ihm „ich will dir heute ein Stück Brot geben, aber dafür will ich dir dein rechtes Auge ausstechen.“
sentences.l: Then the cobbler said to him “I will give you a piece of bread today, but for it I will put out your right eye.”
sentences.i: Then the cobbler said to him, “I will give you a piece of bread today, but in return I will put out your right eye.”
sentences.n: ausstechen is separable and means to put an eye out with a point. dafür is “in exchange for that.” The bargain is stated as flatly as a price, and the tale leaves it so.

sentences.t: Der unglückliche Schneider, der doch gerne sein Leben erhalten wollte, konnte sich nicht anders helfen:
sentences.l: The unlucky tailor, who did gladly want to keep his life, could not help himself otherwise:
sentences.i: The unhappy tailor, who did want to keep his life, could see no other way to help himself.
sentences.n: sich nicht anders helfen können is to have no other way out. The doch inside the clause concedes the obvious: of course he wanted to live.

sentences.t: er weinte noch einmal mit beiden Augen und hielt sie dann hin, und der Schuster, der ein Herz von Stein hatte, stach ihm mit einem scharfen Messer das rechte Auge aus.
sentences.l: he wept once more with both eyes and then held them out, and the cobbler, who had a heart of stone, put out his right eye with a sharp knife.
sentences.i: he wept once more with both eyes and then held them out, and the cobbler, whose heart was stone, gouged out his right eye with a sharp knife.
sentences.n: hinhalten is separable: hielt … hin. stach … aus is the past of the ausstechen of the sentence before, and the dative ihm again says whose eye. The tale does not look away here, and neither does the English.

sentences.t: Dem Schneider kam in den Sinn was ihm sonst seine Mutter gesagt hatte, wenn er in der Speisekammer genascht hatte „essen so viel man mag, und leiden was man muß.“
sentences.l: To the tailor there came into his mind what his mother had otherwise said to him when he had been nibbling in the larder: “eat as much as one likes, and suffer what one must.”
sentences.i: There came into the tailor’s mind what his mother used to say to him when he had been at the sweet things in the larder: “eat as much as you like, and suffer what you must.”
sentences.n: jemandem kommt etwas in den Sinn puts the person it occurs to in the dative. sonst here is “in earlier days, formerly.” naschen is to eat sweet things on the sly. The proverb is two bare infinitives with no subject, and English has to supply one.

sentences.t: Als er sein theuer bezahltes Brot verzehrt hatte, machte er sich wieder auf die Beine, vergaß sein Unglück und tröstete sich damit daß er mit einem Auge noch immer genug sehen könnte.
sentences.l: When he had consumed his dearly paid-for bread, he made himself onto his legs again, forgot his misfortune and comforted himself with the thought that with one eye he could still see enough.
sentences.i: When he had eaten his dearly bought bread, he got on his legs again, forgot his misfortune, and comforted himself that with one eye he could still see well enough.
sentences.n: sich auf die Beine machen is to get going. theuer is the 1857 spelling of teuer. sich damit trösten daß needs an English “with the thought that,” which the German leaves implied; könnte is subjunctive because it reports his own consoling thought.

sentences.t: Aber am sechsten Tag meldete sich der Hunger aufs neue und zehrte ihm fast das Herz auf.
sentences.l: But on the sixth day the hunger announced itself anew and almost ate his heart up.
sentences.i: But on the sixth day hunger made itself felt anew and all but ate his heart away.
sentences.n: sich melden is to report in, to make itself felt. aufzehren is separable: zehrte … auf; and the dative ihm again stands where English puts “his.”

sentences.t: Er fiel Abends bei einem Baum nieder, und am siebenten Morgen konnte er sich vor Mattigkeit nicht erheben, und der Tod saß ihm im Nacken.
sentences.l: He fell down by a tree in the evening, and on the seventh morning he could not raise himself for faintness, and death sat him in the neck.
sentences.i: In the evening he fell down beside a tree, and on the seventh morning he could not raise himself for faintness, and death was sitting at his neck.
sentences.n: niederfallen is separable: fiel … nieder. jemandem im Nacken sitzen is the fixed image for something close behind and about to have you, with the dative ihm carrying “his.”

sentences.t: Da sagte der Schuster „ich will Barmherzigkeit ausüben und dir nochmals Brot geben;
sentences.l: Then the cobbler said “I will exercise mercy and give you bread once more;
sentences.i: Then the cobbler said, “I will show mercy and give you bread once more;
sentences.n: Barmherzigkeit ausüben is the churchly phrase for performing a work of mercy; in his mouth it is a sneer.

sentences.t: umsonst bekommst du es nicht, ich steche dir dafür das andere Auge noch aus.“
sentences.l: for nothing you will not get it, I will put your other eye out for it as well.”
sentences.i: you shall not have it for nothing — I will put out your other eye for it into the bargain.”
sentences.n: umsonst is “for nothing, free of charge” here, not its other sense “in vain.” The present steche stands for the future, as German commonly lets it.

sentences.t: Da erkannte der Schneider sein leichtsinniges Leben, bat den lieben Gott um Verzeihung und sprach „thue was du mußt, ich will leiden was ich muß;
sentences.l: Then the tailor recognised his heedless life, asked dear God for forgiveness and said “do what you must, I will suffer what I must;
sentences.i: Then the tailor saw his heedless life for what it was, begged dear God for forgiveness, and said, “Do what you must; I will suffer what I must;
sentences.n: thue is the 1857 spelling of tue, from thun (modern tun). He answers the cobbler in the shape of his mother’s proverb from a few lines back, keeping leiden was man muß intact.

sentences.t: aber bedenke daß unser Herrgott nicht jeden Augenblick richtet und daß eine andere Stunde kommt, wo die böse That vergolten wird, die du an mir verübst und die ich nicht an dir verdient habe.
sentences.l: but consider that our Lord God does not judge at every moment and that another hour comes, when the evil deed will be repaid that you commit on me and that I have not deserved of you.
sentences.i: but consider that our Lord God does not judge at every moment, and that another hour will come when the evil deed you commit on me, and have not deserved of me, will be paid back.
sentences.n: That is the 1857 spelling of Tat. vergolten wird is the passive of vergelten, to repay — the very verb the three grateful creatures will use of their own debts. Both relative clauses hang on die böse That and are pushed to the end of the sentence.

sentences.t: Ich habe in guten Tagen mit dir getheilt was ich hatte.
sentences.l: I have in good days shared with you what I had.
sentences.i: In good days I shared with you what I had.
sentences.n: getheilt is the 1857 spelling of geteilt, and the perfect tense here does duty for a plain past, as it does in speech.

sentences.t: Mein Handwerk ist der Art daß Stich muß Stich vertreiben.
sentences.l: My trade is of the kind that stitch must drive out stitch.
sentences.i: My trade is of such a kind that stitch must drive out stitch.
sentences.n: der Art is a genitive of quality, “of that kind.” Stich is both the stitch of a needle and a stab with a point, and the tailor’s saying turns on the double sense: the needle is his living, and it is a knife point that has taken his eyes.

sentences.t: Wenn ich keine Augen mehr habe, und nicht mehr nähen kann, so muß ich betteln gehen.
sentences.l: When I have no eyes any more, and can sew no more, then I must go begging.
sentences.i: When I have no eyes left and can sew no more, I must go begging.
sentences.n: betteln gehen sets two verbs side by side with no zu, as German does with gehen — compare schlafen gehen.

sentences.t: Laß mich nur, wenn ich blind bin, hier nicht allein liegen, sonst muß ich verschmachten.“
sentences.l: Only do not let me lie here alone, when I am blind, otherwise I must waste away.”
sentences.i: Only, when I am blind, do not leave me lying here alone, or I shall waste away.”
sentences.n: nur softens the command into a plea. liegen lassen is “to leave lying.” verschmachten is to perish from hunger and thirst — the word returns at the very end of the tale, of the cobbler.

sentences.t: Der Schuster aber, der Gott aus seinem Herzen vertrieben hatte, nahm das Messer und stach ihm noch das linke Auge aus.
sentences.l: The cobbler, however, who had driven God out of his heart, took the knife and put out his left eye as well.
sentences.i: But the cobbler, who had driven God out of his heart, took the knife and put out his left eye too.
sentences.n: vertrieben is from vertreiben, the same verb the tailor had just used of stitch driving out stitch.

sentences.t: Dann gab er ihm ein Stück Brot zu essen, reichte ihm einen Stock und führte ihn hinter sich her.
sentences.l: Then he gave him a piece of bread to eat, handed him a stick and led him along behind himself.
sentences.i: Then he gave him a piece of bread to eat, handed him a stick, and led him along behind him.
sentences.n: hinter sich her führen — the two little words hinter … her give the picture: the blinded man in tow at the end of the stick.

sentences.t: Als die Sonne untergieng, kamen sie aus dem Wald, und vor dem Wald auf dem Feld stand ein Galgen.
sentences.l: When the sun went down, they came out of the forest, and before the forest on the field stood a gallows.
sentences.i: As the sun was going down they came out of the forest, and in front of the forest, on the open field, stood a gallows.
sentences.n: untergieng is the 1857 spelling of unterging, from untergehen, separable. A gallows stood outside the town on open ground, in plain sight of the road.

sentences.t: Dahin leitete der Schuster den blinden Schneider, ließ ihn dann liegen und gieng seiner Wege.
sentences.l: Thither the cobbler led the blind tailor, then let him lie and went his ways.
sentences.i: The cobbler led the blind tailor there, then left him lying and went his way.
sentences.n: seiner Wege gehen is a fixed genitive phrase, “to go one’s way.” liegen lassen is “to leave lying,” as in the tailor’s plea a moment before — the cobbler leaves him exactly as he begged not to be left.

sentences.t: Vor Müdigkeit, Schmerz und Hunger schlief der Unglückliche ein und schlief die ganze Nacht.
sentences.l: From weariness, pain and hunger the unlucky man fell asleep and slept the whole night.
sentences.i: From weariness, pain and hunger the unfortunate man fell asleep and slept the whole night through.
sentences.n: einschlafen, to fall asleep, and schlafen, to sleep, stand side by side, and English needs two verbs as well. der Unglückliche is an adjective used as a noun.

sentences.t: Als der Tag dämmerte, erwachte er, wußte aber nicht wo er lag.
sentences.l: When the day dawned, he awoke, but did not know where he lay.
sentences.n: dämmern is used of dawn and of dusk alike; here the day is coming up.

sentences.t: An dem Galgen hiengen zwei arme Sünder, und auf dem Kopfe eines jeden saß eine Krähe.
sentences.l: On the gallows hung two poor sinners, and on the head of each one sat a crow.
sentences.i: Two poor sinners were hanging on the gallows, and on the head of each sat a crow.
sentences.n: hiengen is the 1857 spelling of hingen. arme Sünder, “poor sinners,” is the ordinary term for the condemned; the executed were left hanging as a warning.

sentences.t: Da fieng der eine an zu sprechen „Bruder, wachst du?“
sentences.l: Then the one began to speak “brother, are you awake?”
sentences.i: Then the one of them began to speak: “Brother, are you awake?”
sentences.n: wachen is “to be awake, to keep watch,” not aufwachen, to wake up. The tale lets the hanged men talk without a word of explanation, and it is left standing so.

sentences.t: „Ja, ich wache“ antwortete der zweite.
sentences.l: “Yes, I am awake” answered the second.
sentences.n: The 1857 text sets no comma before the speech tag here; the quotation simply ends and the tag follows.

sentences.t: „So will ich dir etwas sagen,“ fieng der erste wieder an, „der Thau der heute Nacht über uns vom Galgen herabgefallen ist, der gibt jedem, der sich damit wäscht, die Augen wieder.
sentences.l: “Then I will tell you something,” the first began again, “the dew that has fallen down over us tonight from the gallows, it gives every one who washes himself with it his eyes again.
sentences.i: “Then I will tell you something,” the first began again; “the dew that has fallen from the gallows over us tonight gives every man who washes himself in it his eyes back again.
sentences.n: Thau is the 1857 spelling of Tau. The long subject is picked up again by der before the verb — the resumptive pronoun of spoken German. heute Nacht is “last night” when the night is just over.

sentences.t: Wenn das die Blinden wüßten, wie mancher könnte sein Gesicht wieder haben, der nicht glaubt daß das möglich sei.“
sentences.l: If the blind knew that, how many a one could have his sight again who does not believe that it is possible.”
sentences.i: If the blind knew that, how many a one who does not believe it possible could have his sight back.”
sentences.n: Gesicht is here “eyesight,” its older sense, and not “face” — the same word stands for the face elsewhere in this tale. wüßten is the subjunctive of the unreal condition and sei the subjunctive of the reported belief; mancher is “many a one.”

sentences.t: Als der Schneider das hörte, nahm er sein Taschentuch, drückte es auf das Gras, und als es mit dem Thau befeuchtet war, wusch er seine Augenhöhlen damit.
sentences.l: When the tailor heard that, he took his handkerchief, pressed it on the grass, and when it was moistened with the dew, he washed his eye-sockets with it.
sentences.i: When the tailor heard that, he took his handkerchief, pressed it on the grass, and when it was wet with the dew, washed his eye sockets with it.
sentences.n: befeuchtet is a past participle used as a predicate, a state rather than an action. Augenhöhlen is a compound: Auge plus Höhle, a hollow.

sentences.t: Alsbald gieng in Erfüllung was der Gehenkte gesagt hatte, und ein paar frische und gesunde Augen füllten die Höhlen.
sentences.l: At once there went into fulfilment what the hanged man had said, and a couple of fresh and sound eyes filled the hollows.
sentences.i: At once what the hanged man had said came true, and a pair of fresh, sound eyes filled the sockets.
sentences.n: in Erfüllung gehen is the set phrase for a saying coming true. der Gehenkte is the participle of henken used as a noun, the hanged man. ein paar, small p, is “a couple of” — with eyes it amounts to a pair.

sentences.t: Es dauerte nicht lange, so sah der Schneider die Sonne hinter den Bergen aufsteigen:
sentences.l: It lasted not long, then the tailor saw the sun rise up behind the mountains:
sentences.i: It was not long before the tailor saw the sun climbing up behind the mountains.
sentences.n: es dauerte nicht lange, so … is the tales’ way of saying “before long.” sehen takes a bare infinitive with no zu: sah … aufsteigen.

sentences.t: vor ihm in der Ebene lag die große Königsstadt mit ihren prächtigen Thoren und hundert Thürmen, und die goldenen Knöpfe und Kreuze, die auf den Spitzen standen, fiengen an zu glühen.
sentences.l: before him in the plain lay the great king’s-city with its splendid gates and hundred towers, and the golden knobs and crosses that stood on the spires began to glow.
sentences.i: before him in the plain lay the great royal city with its splendid gates and its hundred towers, and the golden balls and crosses standing on the spires began to glow.
sentences.n: Thoren and Thürmen are the 1857 spellings of Toren and Türmen. Die Knöpfe are the gilded balls set under the cross on a church spire. This is the first thing he sees with his new eyes.

sentences.t: Er unterschied jedes Blatt an den Bäumen, erblickte die Vögel, die vorbei flogen, und die Mücken, die in der Luft tanzten.
sentences.l: He distinguished every leaf on the trees, caught sight of the birds that flew past, and the midges that danced in the air.
sentences.i: He could make out every leaf on the trees, and caught sight of the birds flying past and the midges dancing in the air.
sentences.n: unterscheiden is here “to make out” by sight. erblicken is a single catching sight of, stronger than sehen. Mücken are gnats or midges.

sentences.t: Er holte eine Nähnadel aus der Tasche, und als er den Zwirn einfädeln konnte, so gut als er es je gekonnt hatte, so sprang sein Herz vor Freude.
sentences.l: He fetched a sewing needle out of his pocket, and when he could thread the twine as well as he had ever been able to, his heart leapt for joy.
sentences.i: He took a sewing needle out of his pocket, and when he could thread it as well as he ever could in his life, his heart leapt for joy.
sentences.n: einfädeln is separable and stands whole as an infinitive under konnte. gekonnt is the participle of können used on its own, with no second verb. Threading a needle is the test that matters to a tailor.

sentences.t: Er warf sich auf seine Knie, dankte Gott für die erwiesene Gnade und sprach seinen Morgensegen:
sentences.l: He threw himself on his knees, thanked God for the mercy shown and spoke his morning blessing:
sentences.i: He threw himself on his knees, thanked God for the mercy shown him, and said his morning prayer.
sentences.n: erwiesen is the participle of erweisen, to show or render, used as an adjective before Gnade. Der Morgensegen is the set morning prayer.

sentences.t: er vergaß auch nicht für die armen Sünder zu bitten, die da hiengen, wie der Schwengel in der Glocke, und die der Wind aneinander schlug.
sentences.l: he also did not forget to pray for the poor sinners who hung there like the clapper in the bell, and whom the wind knocked against one another.
sentences.i: nor did he forget to pray for the poor sinners hanging there like the clapper in a bell, whom the wind knocked one against the other.
sentences.n: bitten für is to pray for. In the second relative clause die is the object and der Wind the subject: the wind swings them, not the other way about. Der Schwengel is the clapper hanging inside a bell.

sentences.t: Dann nahm er seinen Bündel auf den Rücken, vergaß bald das ausgestandene Herzeleid und gieng unter Singen und Pfeifen weiter.
sentences.l: Then he took his bundle on his back, soon forgot the heart-sorrow he had gone through and went on further with singing and whistling.
sentences.i: Then he shouldered his bundle, soon forgot the heart’s grief he had endured, and went on his way singing and whistling.
sentences.n: ausgestanden is the participle of ausstehen, to endure, used as an adjective. The 1857 text has seinen Bündel, masculine, where modern German makes Bündel neuter. unter Singen und Pfeifen turns both verbs into nouns.

sentences.t: Das erste was ihm begegnete, war ein braunes Füllen, das frei im Felde herumsprang.
sentences.l: The first thing that met him was a brown foal that sprang about freely in the field.
sentences.i: The first thing he met was a brown foal running loose about the field.
sentences.n: das Füllen is the foal — the noun, not the verb füllen, “to fill,” which turns up two paragraphs later in the tailor’s complaint about the sun; the two are spelled alike. begegnen takes the dative: ihm.

sentences.t: Er packte es an der Mähne, wollte sich aufschwingen und in die Stadt reiten.
sentences.l: He seized it by the mane, wanted to swing himself up and ride into the city.
sentences.i: He grabbed it by the mane, meaning to swing himself up and ride into the city.
sentences.n: German says an der Mähne, “at the mane,” where English says “by.” sich aufschwingen is reflexive, and wollte governs both infinitives.

sentences.t: Das Füllen aber bat um seine Freiheit:
sentences.l: The foal, however, asked for its freedom:
sentences.n: bitten um is “to ask for.” The foal speaks and the tale offers no word of surprise; the three grateful creatures begin here.

sentences.t: „ich bin noch zu jung,“ sprach es, „auch ein leichter Schneider wie du bricht mir den Rücken entzwei, laß mich laufen bis ich stark geworden bin.
sentences.l: “I am still too young,” it said, “even a light tailor like you breaks my back in two, let me run until I have grown strong.
sentences.i: “I am still too young,” it said; “even a light tailor like you would break my back in two — let me run until I have grown strong.
sentences.n: The present bricht stands for what would happen, where English needs “would break.” mir is the dative of possession, “my back.” entzwei is “in two.”

sentences.t: Es kommt vielleicht eine Zeit, wo ich dirs lohnen kann.“
sentences.l: There comes perhaps a time when I can repay you for it.”
sentences.i: Perhaps a time will come when I can repay you for it.”
sentences.n: dirs is dir es run together, “repay it to you.” wo does duty for “when” of a point in time, which German allows and English does not.

sentences.t: „Lauf hin,“ sagte der Schneider, „ich sehe du bist auch so ein Springinsfeld.“
sentences.l: “Run along,” said the tailor, “I see you are such a leap-into-the-field too.”
sentences.i: “Off with you,” said the tailor, “I see you are as much a scamper-about as I am.”
sentences.n: Springinsfeld is a whole phrase made into a noun — spring ins Feld, “jump into the field” — for a harum-scarum young thing. The auch means the tailor counts himself one as well.

sentences.t: Er gab ihm noch einen Hieb mit der Gerte über den Rücken, daß es vor Freude mit den Hinterbeinen ausschlug, über Hecken und Gräben setzte und in das Feld hineinjagte.
sentences.l: He gave it a stroke with the switch over the back besides, so that for joy it kicked out with its hind legs, set over hedges and ditches and raced off into the field.
sentences.i: He gave it a flick of the switch across the back into the bargain, so that for joy it kicked up its hind legs, went over hedges and ditches and raced off into the field.
sentences.n: daß here is “so that,” a result. ausschlagen, to kick out, and hineinjagen, to race in, are both separable; über etwas setzen, of a horse, is to clear it at a jump.

sentences.t: Aber das Schneiderlein hatte seit gestern nichts gegessen.
sentences.l: But the little tailor had eaten nothing since yesterday.
sentences.n: Schneiderlein is the diminutive of Schneider, small size and fondness at once; the tale uses it for him throughout.

sentences.t: „Die Sonne,“ sprach er, „füllt mir zwar die Augen, aber das Brot nicht den Mund.
sentences.l: “The sun,” said he, “fills my eyes, to be sure, but the bread does not fill my mouth.
sentences.i: “The sun,” he said, “fills my eyes well enough, but bread does not fill my mouth.
sentences.n: füllt is the verb füllen, to fill — not das Füllen, the foal of the paragraph before, though the spelling is the same. zwar … aber concedes before it objects. The second half has no verb of its own and borrows füllt, and the dative mir does the work of “my.”

sentences.t: Das erste was mir begegnet und halbweg genießbar ist, das muß herhalten.“
sentences.l: The first thing that meets me and is halfway edible, that must serve.”
sentences.i: The first thing I meet that is halfway fit to eat must go for it.”
sentences.n: herhalten müssen is the set phrase for the one who has to take the consequences. das before muß picks up the long subject again, as so often in speech.

sentences.t: Indem schritt ein Storch ganz ernsthaft über die Wiese daher.
sentences.l: Just then a stork strode along quite gravely over the meadow.
sentences.i: Just then a stork came striding gravely across the meadow.
sentences.n: Indem here is “at that moment,” not the modern conjunction meaning “by doing.” daherschreiten is separable: schritt … daher.

sentences.t: „Halt, halt,“ rief der Schneider und packte ihn am Bein, „ich weiß nicht ob du zu genießen bist, aber mein Hunger erlaubt mir keine lange Wahl, ich muß dir den Kopf abschneiden und dich braten.“
sentences.l: “Stop, stop,” cried the tailor and seized him by the leg, “I do not know whether you are to be eaten, but my hunger allows me no long choosing, I must cut your head off and roast you.”
sentences.i: “Stop, stop,” cried the tailor, catching him by the leg, “I do not know whether you are fit to eat, but my hunger allows me no long choosing — I must cut off your head and roast you.”
sentences.n: zu genießen sein — sein with zu and an infinitive — is a passive of possibility: “is to be eaten, is edible.” dir den Kopf abschneiden uses the dative for the owner where English says “your head.”

sentences.t: „Thue das nicht,“ antwortete der Storch, „ich bin ein heiliger Vogel, dem niemand ein Leid zufügt, und der den Menschen großen Nutzen bringt.
sentences.l: “Do not do that,” answered the stork, “I am a holy bird, to whom nobody does harm, and who brings people great use.
sentences.i: “Do not do that,” answered the stork, “I am a holy bird, whom nobody harms and who is of great use to people.
sentences.n: Thue is the 1857 spelling of tue. jemandem ein Leid zufügen is “to do someone harm,” with the person in the dative — hence the relative dem. Storks were protected birds, held lucky on a roof, and the tale takes that as known.

sentences.t: Läßt du mir mein Leben, so kann ich dirs ein andermal vergelten.“
sentences.l: Do you leave me my life, then I can repay it to you another time.”
sentences.i: If you leave me my life, I can repay you for it another time.”
sentences.n: Another verb-first conditional: Läßt du …, so …. vergelten is the tale’s word for a debt returned, the same the foal used.

sentences.t: „So zieh ab, Vetter Langbein“ sagte der Schneider.
sentences.l: “Then be off, Cousin Longleg,” said the tailor.
sentences.n: abziehen is separable — zieh … ab, an offhand “clear off.” Vetter Langbein is a nickname the tailor coins on the spot, and it sticks: the tale calls the stork that again at the end.

sentences.t: Der Storch erhob sich, ließ die langen Beine hängen und flog gemächlich fort.
sentences.l: The stork raised himself, let his long legs hang and flew away at his leisure.
sentences.i: The stork rose, let his long legs hang, and flew off unhurried.
sentences.n: sich erheben is reflexive, “to rise.” hängen lassen puts two verbs together with no zu; fortfliegen is separable: flog … fort.

sentences.t: „Was soll daraus werden?“ sagte der Schneider zu sich selbst, „mein Hunger wird immer größer und mein Magen immer leerer.
sentences.l: “What is to come of this?” said the tailor to himself, “my hunger grows ever greater and my stomach ever emptier.
sentences.i: “What is to become of this?” said the tailor to himself; “my hunger grows greater and greater and my stomach emptier and emptier.
sentences.n: soll is “is to,” and daraus is “out of it.” immer with a comparative is “ever more, more and more.”

sentences.t: Was mir jetzt in den Weg kommt, das ist verloren.“
sentences.l: What comes into my way now, that is lost.”
sentences.i: Whatever comes in my way now is done for.”
sentences.n: The clause is picked up again by das. verloren sein, of a creature, is “done for.”

sentences.t: Indem sah er auf einem Teich ein paar junge Enten daher schwimmen.
sentences.l: Just then he saw a couple of young ducks come swimming along on a pond.
sentences.i: Just then he saw a few young ducks swimming along on a pond.
sentences.n: sehen with a bare infinitive again: sah … schwimmen. The 1857 text prints daher schwimmen as two words.

sentences.t: „Ihr kommt ja wie gerufen,“ sagte er, packte eine davon, und wollte ihr den Hals umdrehen.
sentences.l: “You come just as if called,” said he, seized one of them, and wanted to twist its neck round.
sentences.i: “You come as if you had been sent for,” said he, and he seized one of them and was about to wring its neck.
sentences.n: wie gerufen kommen is the set phrase for arriving exactly when wanted. The ja inside the clause is not “yes” but a nudge of emphasis, and wollte here is “was about to.”

sentences.t: Da fieng eine alte Ente, die in dem Schilf steckte, laut an zu kreischen, schwamm mit aufgesperrtem Schnabel herbei und bat ihn flehentlich sich ihrer lieben Kinder zu erbarmen.
sentences.l: Then an old duck that was stuck in the reeds began to shriek loudly, swam up with wide-open beak and begged him imploringly to have mercy on her dear children.
sentences.i: Then an old duck that was lurking in the reeds began to shriek aloud, came swimming up with her beak wide open, and begged him imploringly to take pity on her dear children.
sentences.n: sich erbarmen takes the genitive, ihrer lieben Kinder — an old case-use that survives in this verb. stecken is to be stuck, to sit hidden; aufgesperrt is the participle of aufsperren, to open wide.

sentences.t: „Denkst du nicht,“ sagte sie, „wie deine Mutter jammern würde, wenn dich einer wegholen und dir den Garaus machen wollte.“
sentences.l: “Do you not think,” said she, “how your mother would lament if someone wanted to carry you off and make an end of you.”
sentences.i: “Do you not think,” said she, “how your mother would wail if somebody were to carry you off and make an end of you?”
sentences.n: jemandem den Garaus machen is the old fixed phrase for finishing someone off; Garaus is “all out,” once the call that closed the day. einer is “someone.” The 1857 text prints the question with a full stop.

sentences.t: „Sei nur still,“ sagte der gutmüthige Schneider, „du sollst deine Kinder behalten,“ und setzte die Gefangene wieder ins Wasser.
sentences.l: “Only be quiet,” said the good-natured tailor, “you shall keep your children,” and set the captive back into the water.
sentences.i: “Be still,” said the good-natured tailor, “you shall keep your children,” and he set the prisoner back in the water.
sentences.n: gutmüthige is the 1857 spelling of gutmütige. die Gefangene is an adjective made into a noun, feminine, “the captured one.” sollst here is a promise, not a command.

sentences.t: Als er sich umkehrte, stand er vor einem alten Baum, der halb hohl war, und sah die wilden Bienen aus- und einfliegen.
sentences.l: When he turned himself round, he stood before an old tree that was half hollow, and saw the wild bees flying out and in.
sentences.i: When he turned round he stood before an old tree that was half hollow, and saw the wild bees flying in and out.
sentences.n: aus- und einfliegen is printed with a hanging hyphen: the aus- stands for ausfliegen and borrows the fliegen of einfliegen. sich umkehren is reflexive, to turn oneself about.

sentences.t: „Da finde ich gleich den Lohn für meine gute That“ sagte der Schneider, „der Honig wird mich laben.“
sentences.l: “There I find at once the reward for my good deed,” said the tailor, “the honey will refresh me.”
sentences.i: “Here I find the reward for my good deed at once,” said the tailor; “the honey will revive me.”
sentences.n: That is the 1857 spelling of Tat. laben is an elevated word for refreshing someone with food or drink.

sentences.t: Aber der Weisel kam heraus, drohte und sprach „wenn du mein Volk anrührst und mein Nest zerstörst, so sollen dir unsere Stacheln wie zehntausend glühende Nadeln in die Haut fahren.
sentences.l: But the queen bee came out, threatened and said “if you touch my people and destroy my nest, then our stings shall drive into your skin like ten thousand glowing needles.
sentences.i: But the queen bee came out, threatened him and said, “If you lay a hand on my people and destroy my nest, our stings shall go into your skin like ten thousand red-hot needles.
sentences.n: Der Weisel is the beekeepers’ old word for the queen of the hive — grammatically masculine, though the bee is a queen — and das Volk is the standing word for the colony. anrühren is separable, but in a subordinate clause it stays joined and stands at the end: anrührst. in die Haut fahren is fahren in its older sense of darting, not travelling.

sentences.t: Läßt du uns aber in Ruhe und gehst deiner Wege, so wollen wir dir ein andermal dafür einen Dienst leisten.“
sentences.l: But do you leave us in peace and go your ways, then we will do you a service for it another time.”
sentences.i: But if you leave us in peace and go your way, we will do you a service for it another time.”
sentences.n: The third verb-first conditional of the tale, and the third creature to promise repayment. einen Dienst leisten is to render a service; deiner Wege gehen is the same genitive phrase used of the cobbler at the gallows.

sentences.t: Das Schneiderlein sah daß auch hier nichts anzufangen war.
sentences.l: The little tailor saw that here too there was nothing to be begun.
sentences.i: The little tailor saw that here too there was nothing to be made of it.
sentences.n: sein with zu and an infinitive is again a passive of possibility: nichts anzufangen war, “nothing was to be started.”

sentences.t: „Drei Schüsseln leer,“ sagte er, „und auf der vierten nichts, das ist eine schlechte Mahlzeit.“
sentences.l: “Three dishes empty,” said he, “and on the fourth nothing, that is a poor meal.”
sentences.i: “Three dishes empty,” said he, “and nothing on the fourth — that is a poor meal.”
sentences.n: He is counting the foal, the stork and the bees, and adds an empty fourth for good measure. The sentence has no verb at all until das ist.

sentences.t: Er schleppte sich also mit seinem ausgehungerten Magen in die Stadt, und da es eben zu Mittag läutete, so war für ihn im Gasthaus schon gekocht und er konnte sich gleich zu Tisch setzen.
sentences.l: So he dragged himself with his famished stomach into the city, and since it was just ringing noon, the cooking was already done for him in the inn and he could set himself straight down to table.
sentences.i: So he dragged himself into the city with his famished stomach, and since noon was just being rung, the meal was already cooked for him at the inn and he could sit down to table at once.
sentences.n: zu Mittag läuten is the midday bell. war … gekocht is an impersonal passive with no subject at all, which English has to fill out. ausgehungert is the participle of aushungern, to starve out.

sentences.t: Als er satt war, sagte er „nun will ich auch arbeiten.“
sentences.l: When he was full, he said “now I will work too.”
sentences.n: satt is “full up, fed” — an everyday German word with no one-word English match.

sentences.t: Er gieng in der Stadt umher, suchte einen Meister und fand auch bald ein gutes Unterkommen.
sentences.l: He went about in the city, sought a master and soon found a good place too.
sentences.i: He went about the city, looked for a master, and soon found a good place.
sentences.n: umhergehen is separable: gieng … umher. Ein Meister is the master craftsman a journeyman hires himself to; das Unterkommen is a situation, a place to work and live.

sentences.t: Da er aber sein Handwerk von Grund aus gelernt hatte, so dauerte es nicht lange, er ward berühmt, und jeder wollte seinen neuen Rock von dem kleinen Schneider gemacht haben.
sentences.l: But since he had learned his trade from the ground up, it did not last long, he became famous, and everyone wanted to have his new coat made by the little tailor.
sentences.i: But since he had learned his trade from the ground up, it was not long before he became famous, and everyone wanted his new coat made by the little tailor.
sentences.n: ward is the old past of werden, “became,” where modern German has wurde. von with the dative names the agent, “by the little tailor.”

sentences.t: Alle Tage nahm sein Ansehen zu.
sentences.l: Every day his standing increased.
sentences.i: His standing grew greater every day.
sentences.n: zunehmen is separable: nahm … zu. Alle Tage is another bare accusative of time.

sentences.t: „Ich kann in meiner Kunst nicht weiter kommen,“ sprach er, „und doch gehts jeden Tag besser.“
sentences.l: “I cannot get further in my art,” said he, “and yet it goes better every day.”
sentences.i: “I can get no further in my craft,” said he, “and yet things go better every day.”
sentences.n: Kunst is the craftsman’s skill, not fine art. gehts is geht es run together, and es geht besser is the impersonal “things are going better.”

sentences.t: Endlich bestellte ihn der König zu seinem Hofschneider.
sentences.l: At last the king appointed him to be his court tailor.
sentences.i: At last the king appointed him his court tailor.
sentences.n: jemanden zu etwas bestellen is to appoint someone as something. Hofschneider is Hof, the court, plus Schneider; the cobbler gets the matching title in the next line.

sentences.t: Aber wies in der Welt geht.
sentences.l: But how it goes in the world.
sentences.i: But that is the way of the world.
sentences.n: wies is wie es run together. The sentence has no main clause at all — it is left hanging as a sigh, and the English has to close it somehow.

sentences.t: An demselben Tag war sein ehemaliger Kamerad, der Schuster, auch Hofschuster geworden.
sentences.l: On the same day his former comrade, the cobbler, had become court cobbler too.
sentences.n: ehemalig is “former.” geworden … war is the pluperfect of werden, “had become.”

sentences.t: Als dieser den Schneider erblickte und sah daß er wieder zwei gesunde Augen hatte, so peinigte ihn das Gewissen.
sentences.l: When this one caught sight of the tailor and saw that he had two sound eyes again, his conscience tormented him.
sentences.i: When the cobbler caught sight of the tailor and saw that he had two sound eyes again, his conscience tormented him.
sentences.n: dieser points back to the last person named, the cobbler; English has to repeat the noun. das Gewissen is the subject and ihn the object — the conscience does the tormenting.

sentences.t: „Ehe er Rache an mir nimmt,“ dachte er bei sich selbst, „muß ich ihm eine Grube graben.“
sentences.l: “Before he takes revenge on me,” he thought to himself, “I must dig him a pit.”
sentences.i: “Before he takes his revenge on me,” he thought to himself, “I must dig a pit for him.”
sentences.n: Rache an jemandem nehmen is to take revenge on someone. jemandem eine Grube graben is proverbial for laying a trap, and the next sentence completes the proverb.

sentences.t: Wer aber andern eine Grube gräbt, fällt selbst hinein.
sentences.l: But whoever digs a pit for others falls into it himself.
sentences.n: The proverb comes from the Book of Proverbs and was as familiar in German as in English. The tale states it here and then lets the plot prove it.

sentences.t: Abends, als er Feierabend gemacht hatte, und es dämmerig geworden war, schlich er sich zu dem König und sagte „Herr König, der Schneider ist ein übermüthiger Mensch, und hat sich vermessen er wollte die goldene Krone wieder herbei schaffen, die vor alten Zeiten ist verloren gegangen.“
sentences.l: In the evening, when he had knocked off work and it had grown dusky, he crept to the king and said “Lord King, the tailor is an overweening fellow, and has presumed he would fetch back the golden crown that was lost in olden times.”
sentences.i: In the evening, when he had finished work and it had grown dusk, he crept to the king and said, “My lord King, the tailor is an overweening fellow, and he has boasted that he would bring back the golden crown that was lost in the old days.”
sentences.n: Feierabend machen is to stop work for the day. sich vermessen is “to presume, to boast that one can do a thing,” and it is the cobbler’s word every time he lies to the king. wollte reports the tailor’s supposed words: “that he would.”

sentences.t: „Das sollte mir lieb sein“ sprach der König, ließ den Schneider am andern Morgen vor sich fordern und befahl ihm die Krone wieder herbeizuschaffen, oder für immer die Stadt zu verlassen.
sentences.l: “That should be dear to me,” said the king, had the tailor summoned before him the next morning and commanded him to fetch the crown back, or to leave the city for ever.
sentences.i: “That would please me,” said the king, and the next morning he had the tailor summoned before him and ordered him to bring the crown back or leave the city for good.
sentences.n: das sollte mir lieb sein is a set courteous phrase, “I should be glad of that.” lassen with an infinitive is “to have something done”: ließ … fordern.

sentences.t: „Oho,“ dachte der Schneider, „ein Schelm gibt mehr als er hat.
sentences.l: “Oho,” thought the tailor, “a rogue gives more than he has.
sentences.i: “Oho,” thought the tailor, “a rogue promises more than he has.
sentences.n: The proverb means that a man who offers what he cannot deliver is a knave — the tailor sees at once that someone has promised in his name. geben here is closer to offering than to a gift, which is why the idiomatic line says “promises.”

sentences.t: Wenn der murrköpfige König von mir verlangt was kein Mensch leisten kann, so will ich nicht warten bis morgen, sondern gleich heute wieder zur Stadt hinaus wandern.“
sentences.l: If the grumble-headed king demands of me what no person can perform, then I will not wait until tomorrow, but wander out of the city again this very day.”
sentences.i: If the crabbed king demands of me what no man alive can perform, I will not wait till tomorrow, but walk out of the city again this very day.”
sentences.n: murrköpfig is built from murren, to grumble, and Kopf — a grumble-head. zur Stadt hinaus is “out of the city,” the zu marking the gate one goes through.

sentences.t: Er schnürte also sein Bündel, als er aber aus dem Thor heraus war, so that es ihm doch leid daß er sein Glück aufgeben und die Stadt, in der es ihm so wohl gegangen war, mit dem Rücken ansehen sollte.
sentences.l: So he laced up his bundle, but when he was out of the gate, it did grieve him that he should give up his fortune and look at the city, in which it had gone so well with him, with his back.
sentences.i: So he tied up his bundle, but once he was outside the gate it did grieve him that he should give up his good fortune and turn his back on the city where things had gone so well with him.
sentences.n: es thut mir leid is “I am sorry,” with the person in the dative. etwas mit dem Rücken ansehen — to look at a thing with one’s back — is the old way of saying you turn your back on it. Thor is the 1857 spelling of Tor.

sentences.t: Er kam zu dem Teich, wo er mit den Enten Bekanntschaft gemacht hatte, da saß gerade die Alte, der er ihre Jungen gelassen hatte, am Ufer und putzte sich mit dem Schnabel.
sentences.l: He came to the pond where he had made acquaintance with the ducks; there sat just then the old one, to whom he had left her young, on the bank and preened herself with her beak.
sentences.i: He came to the pond where he had made the ducks’ acquaintance, and there on the bank sat the very old duck whose young he had left her, preening herself with her beak.
sentences.n: der er ihre Jungen gelassen hatte — der is the dative relative, “to whom,” and German keeps the possessive ihre besides. sich putzen is to preen, to clean oneself.

sentences.t: Sie erkannte ihn gleich, und fragte warum er den Kopf so hängen lasse.
sentences.l: She recognised him at once, and asked why he let his head hang so.
sentences.i: She knew him at once, and asked why he let his head hang so.
sentences.n: lasse is the subjunctive of reported speech: the question is passed on rather than quoted, and German marks that with the verb form where English does not. den Kopf hängen lassen is to be downcast.

sentences.t: „Du wirst dich nicht wundern, wenn du hörst was mir begegnet ist“ antwortete der Schneider und erzählte ihr sein Schicksal.
sentences.l: “You will not wonder when you hear what has happened to me,” answered the tailor and told her his fate.
sentences.i: “You will not wonder when you hear what has befallen me,” answered the tailor, and he told her his story.
sentences.n: sich wundern is reflexive, “to be surprised.” begegnen, which was “to meet” of the foal and the stork, is here “to befall.”

sentences.t: „Wenns weiter nichts ist,“ sagte die Ente, „da können wir Rath schaffen.
sentences.l: “If it is nothing more than that,” said the duck, “then we can find counsel.
sentences.i: “If that is all it is,” said the duck, “we can find a remedy.
sentences.n: Wenns is wenn es. Rath schaffen — Rath is the 1857 spelling of Rat — is to provide a way out, not advice in words.

sentences.t: Die Krone ist ins Wasser gefallen und liegt unten auf dem Grund, wie bald haben wir sie wieder heraufgeholt.
sentences.l: The crown has fallen into the water and lies below on the bottom; how soon we shall have fetched it up again.
sentences.i: The crown fell into the water and is lying down on the bottom — we shall have it up again in no time.
sentences.n: wie bald … is an exclamation of how easy the thing is. heraufholen is separable, and its parts stand joined in the participle heraufgeholt.

sentences.t: Breite nur derweil dein Taschentuch ans Ufer aus.“
sentences.l: Only spread out your handkerchief on the bank meanwhile.”
sentences.i: Just spread your handkerchief out on the bank meanwhile.”
sentences.n: ausbreiten is separable and the particle waits at the end: Breite … aus. derweil is “meanwhile,” now old-fashioned.

sentences.t: Sie tauchte mit ihren zwölf Jungen unter, und nach fünf Minuten war sie wieder oben und saß mitten in der Krone, die auf ihren Fittigen ruhte, und die zwölf Jungen schwammen rund herum, hatten ihre Schnäbel untergelegt und halfen tragen.
sentences.l: She dived under with her twelve young, and after five minutes she was up again and sat in the middle of the crown, which rested on her pinions, and the twelve young swam round about, had laid their beaks underneath and helped to carry.
sentences.i: She dived under with her twelve young, and after five minutes she was up again, sitting in the middle of the crown, which rested on her pinions, while the twelve young swam round about with their beaks pushed underneath, helping to carry.
sentences.n: untertauchen is separable: tauchte … unter. Fittige is an elevated word for wings, the one used of angels. helfen takes a bare infinitive with no zu: halfen tragen.

sentences.t: Sie schwammen ans Land und legten die Krone auf das Tuch.
sentences.l: They swam to land and laid the crown on the cloth.
sentences.n: legen is the transitive “to lay,” beside liegen, “to lie” — a pair German keeps carefully apart.

sentences.t: Du glaubst nicht wie prächtig die Krone war, wenn die Sonne darauf schien, so glänzte sie wie hunderttausend Karfunkelsteine.
sentences.l: You would not believe how splendid the crown was; when the sun shone on it, it gleamed like a hundred thousand carbuncle stones.
sentences.i: You would not believe how splendid the crown was — when the sun shone on it, it gleamed like a hundred thousand carbuncles.
sentences.n: The narrator turns and speaks to the reader as du, the one place in the tale where that happens. Ein Karfunkelstein is the old name for a deep red gem, a garnet or ruby, believed to glow of itself.

sentences.t: Der Schneider band sein Tuch mit den vier Zipfeln zusammen und trug sie zum König, der in einer Freude war und dem Schneider eine goldene Kette um den Hals hieng.
sentences.l: The tailor bound his cloth together by the four corners and carried it to the king, who was in such a joy and hung a golden chain about the tailor’s neck.
sentences.i: The tailor knotted his cloth together by its four corners and carried it to the king, who was overjoyed and hung a golden chain about the tailor’s neck.
sentences.n: zusammenbinden is separable: band … zusammen. trug sie refers to die Krone, feminine, not to the cloth. in einer Freude sein, with the article, is stronger than plain Freude — beside himself with it. hieng is the 1857 spelling of hing.

sentences.t: Als der Schuster sah daß der eine Streich mislungen war, so besann er sich auf einen zweiten, trat vor den König und sprach „Herr König, der Schneider ist wieder so übermüthig geworden, er vermißt sich das ganze königliche Schloß mit allem was darin ist, los und fest, innen und außen, in Wachs abzubilden.“
sentences.l: When the cobbler saw that the one trick had failed, he bethought himself of a second, stepped before the king and said “Lord King, the tailor has grown so overweening again, he presumes to model the whole royal castle in wax with everything that is in it, loose and fixed, inside and outside.”
sentences.i: When the cobbler saw that the first trick had failed, he bethought himself of a second, stepped before the king and said, “My lord King, the tailor has grown overweening again — he presumes to model the whole royal castle in wax, with everything in it, loose and fixed, inside and out.”
sentences.n: mislungen is the 1857 spelling of misslungen, from mislingen, to fail. sich auf etwas besinnen is to hit on, to think of. los und fest — loose and fastened down — is a legal-sounding pair covering movable and immovable goods.

sentences.t: Der König ließ den Schneider kommen und befahl ihm das ganze königliche Schloß mit allem was darin wäre, los und fest, innen und außen, in Wachs abzubilden und wenn er es nicht zu Stande brächte, oder es fehlte nur ein Nagel an der Wand, so sollte er zeitlebens unter der Erde gefangen sitzen.
sentences.l: The king had the tailor come and commanded him to model the whole royal castle in wax with everything that was in it, loose and fixed, inside and outside, and if he did not bring it about, or there were but one nail missing on the wall, he should sit imprisoned under the earth his life long.
sentences.i: The king had the tailor fetched and ordered him to model the whole royal castle in wax with everything in it, loose and fixed, inside and out; and if he did not bring it off, or so much as a nail were missing from the wall, he should sit imprisoned underground for the rest of his life.
sentences.n: wäre, brächte and fehlte are subjunctives carrying the king’s command over into reported speech. zu Stande bringen (modern zustande) is to bring off, to accomplish; zeitlebens is “for a lifetime.” The cobbler’s words are repeated back almost unchanged, which is how the tale shows the trap closing.

sentences.t: Der Schneider dachte „es kommt immer ärger, das hält kein Mensch aus,“ warf sein Bündel auf den Rücken und wanderte fort.
sentences.l: The tailor thought “it comes ever worse, no person can bear that,” threw his bundle on his back and wandered off.
sentences.i: The tailor thought, “It gets worse and worse — no man alive could bear it,” threw his bundle on his back and set off.
sentences.n: ärger is the comparative of arg, bad — worse in the sense of more outrageous. aushalten is separable: hält … aus.

sentences.t: Als er an den hohlen Baum kam, setzte er sich nieder und ließ den Kopf hängen.
sentences.l: When he came to the hollow tree, he set himself down and let his head hang.
sentences.i: When he came to the hollow tree he sat down and let his head hang.
sentences.n: sich niedersetzen is separable and reflexive at once: setzte sich nieder. The hanging head is the same phrase the duck used of him.

sentences.t: Die Bienen kamen heraus geflogen, und der Weisel fragte ihn ob er einen steifen Hals hätte, weil er den Kopf so schief hielt.
sentences.l: The bees came flying out, and the queen asked him whether he had a stiff neck, because he held his head so crooked.
sentences.i: The bees came flying out, and the queen bee asked whether he had a stiff neck, since he held his head so crookedly.
sentences.n: kamen … geflogen — kommen with a past participle is the German way of saying “came flying.” hätte is the subjunctive of the reported question. The dry joke is the tale’s own.

sentences.t: „Ach nein,“ antwortete der Schneider, „mich drückt etwas anderes,“ und erzählte was der König von ihm gefordert hatte.
sentences.l: “Ah no,” answered the tailor, “something else presses me,” and told what the king had demanded of him.
sentences.i: “Ah no,” answered the tailor, “it is something else that weighs on me,” and he told what the king had demanded of him.
sentences.n: mich drückt etwas anderes puts the object first, exactly as with the cobbler and his bread in the forest: the thing does the pressing and the person is pressed.

sentences.t: Die Bienen fiengen an unter einander zu summen und zu brummen, und der Weisel sprach „geh nur wieder nach Haus, komm aber Morgen um diese Zeit wieder und bring ein großes Tuch mit, so wird alles gut gehen.“
sentences.l: The bees began to hum and to buzz among one another, and the queen said “only go home again, but come again tomorrow at this time and bring a large cloth with you, then all will go well.”
sentences.i: The bees began to hum and buzz among themselves, and the queen said, “Just go home again, but come back tomorrow at this hour and bring a large cloth with you, and all will go well.”
sentences.n: summen and brummen are a sound-pair, the high hum and the low, and German likes such rhyming pairs. mitbringen is separable: bring … mit. The 1857 text capitalises Morgen where modern German writes morgen, “tomorrow.”

sentences.t: Da kehrte er wieder um, die Bienen aber flogen nach dem königlichen Schloß, geradezu in die offenen Fenster hinein, krochen in allen Ecken herum und besahen alles aufs genauste.
sentences.l: Then he turned round again, but the bees flew to the royal castle, straight into the open windows, crept about in all the corners and looked over everything most exactly.
sentences.i: So he turned back again, but the bees flew off to the royal castle, straight in at the open windows, crept about in every corner and examined everything most closely.
sentences.n: umkehren, hineinfliegen and herumkriechen are all separable, and each drops its particle to the end of its clause. aufs genauste is a superlative used adverbially, “in the most exact way.”

sentences.t: Dann liefen sie zurück und bildeten das Schloß in Wachs nach mit einer solchen Geschwindigkeit, daß man meinte es wüchse einem vor den Augen.
sentences.l: Then they ran back and modelled the castle after it in wax with such a speed that one thought it were growing before one’s eyes.
sentences.i: Then they ran back and copied the castle in wax with such speed that you would have thought it was growing before your eyes.
sentences.n: nachbilden is separable — bildeten … nach, modelled after the original. wüchse is the subjunctive of wachsen inside the reported thought, and einem is the dative of man, “before one’s eyes.”
