sentences.t: Schon am Abend war alles fertig, und als der Schneider am folgenden Morgen kam, so stand das ganze prächtige Gebäude da, und es fehlte kein Nagel an der Wand und keine Ziegel auf dem Dach;
sentences.l: Already by evening everything was finished, and when the tailor came the following morning, the whole splendid building stood there, and not a nail was missing on the wall and no tile on the roof;
sentences.i: By evening everything was finished, and when the tailor came the next morning the whole splendid building stood there, with not a nail missing from the wall nor a tile from the roof;
sentences.n: dastehen is separable: stand … da. The 1857 text has keine Ziegel, feminine, where modern German makes Ziegel masculine; a roof tile is meant.

sentences.t: dabei war es zart und schneeweiß, und roch süß wie Honig.
sentences.l: and with all that it was delicate and snow-white, and smelled sweet as honey.
sentences.i: and withal it was delicate and snow-white, and smelled sweet as honey.
sentences.n: dabei ties the clause back to what precedes: “and along with that.” The wax gives itself away by its scent.

sentences.t: Der Schneider packte es vorsichtig in sein Tuch und brachte es dem König, der aber konnte sich nicht genug verwundern, stellte es in seinem größten Saal auf und schenkte dem Schneider dafür ein großes steinernes Haus.
sentences.l: The tailor packed it carefully in his cloth and brought it to the king, but he could not wonder at it enough, set it up in his largest hall and made the tailor a present of a great stone house for it.
sentences.i: The tailor packed it carefully in his cloth and brought it to the king, who could not wonder at it enough; he set it up in his largest hall and gave the tailor a great stone house for it.
sentences.n: der aber picks the king up again as a fresh subject, which spoken German prefers to continuing the relative clause. aufstellen is separable: stellte … auf. steinern is the adjective from Stein, “of stone.”

sentences.t: Der Schuster aber ließ nicht nach, gieng zum drittenmal zu dem König und sprach „Herr König, dem Schneider ist zu Ohren gekommen daß auf dem Schloßhof kein Wasser springen will, da hat er sich vermessen es solle mitten im Hof mannshoch aufsteigen und hell sein wie Krystall.“
sentences.l: The cobbler, however, did not let up, went to the king for the third time and said “Lord King, it has come to the tailor’s ears that no water will spring in the castle yard, so he has presumed it shall rise a man’s height in the middle of the yard and be clear as crystal.”
sentences.i: But the cobbler did not let up; he went to the king a third time and said, “My lord King, it has come to the tailor’s ears that no water will rise in the castle yard, and so he has boasted that it shall spring up a man’s height in the middle of the yard and be clear as crystal.”
sentences.n: nachlassen is separable: ließ … nach. jemandem zu Ohren kommen is “to reach someone’s ears,” with the person in the dative. solle is the subjunctive of reported speech; mannshoch is “as high as a man,” and Krystall is the 1857 spelling of Kristall.

sentences.t: Da ließ der König den Schneider herbei holen und sagte „wenn nicht Morgen ein Strahl von Wasser in meinem Hof springt, wie du versprochen hast, so soll dich der Scharfrichter auf demselben Hof um einen Kopf kürzer machen.“
sentences.l: Then the king had the tailor fetched and said “if tomorrow no jet of water springs in my yard, as you have promised, then the executioner shall make you a head shorter in that same yard.”
sentences.i: Then the king had the tailor fetched and said, “If tomorrow no jet of water springs up in my yard, as you have promised, the executioner shall make you a head shorter in that same yard.”
sentences.n: um einen Kopf kürzer machen — to make shorter by a head — is the standing grim joke for beheading, with um marking the measure of difference. Der Scharfrichter is the executioner.

sentences.t: Der arme Schneider besann sich nicht lange und eilte zum Thore hinaus, und weil es ihm diesmal ans Leben gehen sollte, so rollten ihm die Thränen über die Backen herab.
sentences.l: The poor tailor did not think long and hurried out of the gate, and because this time it was to go at his life, the tears rolled down over his cheeks.
sentences.i: The poor tailor did not stop to think and hurried out of the gate, and because this time his life was at stake, the tears rolled down his cheeks.
sentences.n: es geht jemandem ans Leben is the set phrase for a matter of life and death. Thore and Thränen are the 1857 spellings of Tore and Tränen, and the dative ihm again supplies “his.”

sentences.t: Indem er so voll Trauer dahin gieng, kam das Füllen herangesprungen, dem er einmal die Freiheit geschenkt hatte, und aus dem ein hübscher Brauner geworden war.
sentences.l: As he went along so full of sorrow, the foal came springing up, to which he had once given its freedom, and out of which a handsome brown horse had become.
sentences.i: As he was going along so full of sorrow, up came springing the foal to which he had once given its freedom, and which had grown into a handsome bay.
sentences.n: Indem here is the conjunction “while,” unlike the Indem earlier in the tale that meant “just then.” ein Brauner is an adjective made into a noun for a brown horse. Both relative clauses trail after the verb at the end of the sentence.

sentences.t: „Jetzt kommt die Stunde,“ sprach er zu ihm, „wo ich dir deine Gutthat vergelten kann.
sentences.l: “Now comes the hour,” he said to him, “when I can repay you your good deed.
sentences.i: “Now the hour has come,” he said to him, “when I can repay you for your good deed.
sentences.n: The 1857 text has sprach er, masculine, of the horse that was das Füllen, neuter, a moment ago: the grammar follows the grown animal rather than the foal. Gutthat is the 1857 spelling of Guttat, a good deed, and wo again does duty for “when.”

sentences.t: Ich weiß schon was dir fehlt, aber es soll dir bald geholfen werden, sitz nur auf, mein Rücken kann deiner zwei tragen.“
sentences.l: I know already what ails you, but you shall soon be helped, only sit up, my back can carry two of you.”
sentences.i: I know already what ails you, but you shall soon be helped — only mount up, my back can carry two of your sort.”
sentences.n: was dir fehlt is the everyday “what is the matter with you,” with the person in the dative. es soll dir geholfen werden is an impersonal passive, since helfen cannot take an accusative object. deiner zwei is a genitive, “two of you,” and aufsitzen is separable: sitz … auf.

sentences.t: Dem Schneider kam das Herz wieder, er sprang in einem Satz auf, und das Pferd rennte in vollem Lauf zur Stadt hinein und geradezu auf den Schloßhof.
sentences.l: To the tailor his heart came back, he sprang up in a single bound, and the horse ran at full speed into the city and straight to the castle yard.
sentences.i: The tailor’s heart came back to him, he sprang up at a single bound, and the horse ran at full speed into the city and straight to the castle yard.
sentences.n: jemandem kommt das Herz wieder puts the person whose courage returns in the dative. rennte is the old weak past of rennen, where modern German has rannte.

sentences.t: Da jagte es dreimal rund herum, schnell wie der Blitz und beim drittenmal stürzte es nieder.
sentences.l: There it raced three times round about, quick as the lightning, and at the third time it plunged down.
sentences.i: There it raced three times round, quick as lightning, and at the third time it plunged down.
sentences.n: es refers to das Pferd, neuter. niederstürzen is separable: stürzte … nieder. Three times round is the tale’s usual magic count.

sentences.t: In dem Augenblick aber krachte es furchtbar:
sentences.l: In that moment, however, it crashed fearfully:
sentences.i: But at that moment there came a fearful crash:
sentences.n: es krachte is impersonal — German lets the empty es do the crashing, where English needs a noun.

sentences.t: ein Stück Erde sprang in der Mitte des Hofs wie eine Kugel in die Luft und über das Schloß hinaus, und gleich dahinter her erhob sich ein Strahl von Wasser so hoch wie Mann und Pferd, und das Wasser war so rein wie Krystall, und die Sonnenstrahlen fiengen an darauf zu tanzen.
sentences.l: a piece of earth sprang up in the middle of the yard like a ball into the air and out over the castle, and immediately behind it there rose a jet of water as high as man and horse, and the water was as pure as crystal, and the sunbeams began to dance on it.
sentences.i: a lump of earth flew up in the middle of the yard like a cannon ball, into the air and out over the castle, and straight behind it rose a jet of water as high as man and horse; and the water was as pure as crystal, and the sunbeams began to dance upon it.
sentences.n: Eine Kugel is a ball, and of a shot a cannon ball, which the idiomatic line makes explicit. des Hofs is the genitive, “of the yard,” and dahinter her is “along behind it.”

sentences.t: Als der König das sah, stand er vor Verwunderung auf, gieng und umarmte das Schneiderlein im Angesicht aller Menschen.
sentences.l: When the king saw that, he stood up in astonishment, went and embraced the little tailor in the sight of all people.
sentences.i: When the king saw that, he stood up in astonishment, went over and embraced the little tailor in the sight of all the people.
sentences.n: vor Verwunderung is again vor giving the cause of a bodily reaction. im Angesicht is elevated, “before the eyes of.” aufstehen is separable: stand … auf.

sentences.t: Aber das Glück dauerte nicht lang.
sentences.l: But the good fortune did not last long.
sentences.n: das Glück is luck and happiness at once, and the tale plays on both senses throughout.

sentences.t: Der König hatte Töchter genug, eine immer schöner als die andere, aber keinen Sohn.
sentences.l: The king had daughters enough, one always more beautiful than the other, but no son.
sentences.i: The king had daughters enough, each one lovelier than the last, but no son.
sentences.n: immer with a comparative again: eine immer schöner als die andere is a fixed formula in the tales for a whole row of them.

sentences.t: Da begab sich der boshafte Schuster zum viertenmal zu dem Könige, und sprach „Herr König, der Schneider läßt nicht ab von seinem Übermuth.
sentences.l: Then the malicious cobbler betook himself to the king for the fourth time, and said “Lord King, the tailor does not leave off from his overweening.
sentences.i: Then the spiteful cobbler betook himself to the king for the fourth time and said, “My lord King, the tailor does not leave off his overweening ways.
sentences.n: sich begeben is an elevated “to betake oneself.” dem Könige carries the old dative -e, still usual in 1857. ablassen von is to desist from; Übermuth (modern Übermut) is the arrogance of one who has had too much good luck.

sentences.t: Jetzt hat er sich vermessen, wenn er wolle, so könne er dem Herrn König einen Sohn durch die Lüfte herbei tragen lassen.“
sentences.l: Now he has presumed that, if he wished, he could have a son carried to the lord king through the airs.”
sentences.i: Now he has boasted that if he chose, he could have a son brought to my lord King through the air.”
sentences.n: wolle and könne are subjunctives of reported speech, marking the whole clause as the cobbler’s report of what the tailor is supposed to have said. die Lüfte is the plural of Luft, used of the open sky; tragen lassen is “to have carried.”

sentences.t: Der König ließ den Schneider rufen und sprach „wenn du mir binnen neun Tagen einen Sohn bringen läßt, so sollst du meine älteste Tochter zur Frau haben.“
sentences.l: The king had the tailor called and said “if within nine days you have a son brought to me, then you shall have my eldest daughter to wife.”
sentences.i: The king had the tailor called and said, “If within nine days you have a son brought to me, you shall have my eldest daughter to wife.”
sentences.n: binnen with the dative is “within” a stretch of time. zur Frau haben is the set marriage phrase, “to have as wife.”

sentences.t: „Der Lohn ist freilich groß,“ dachte das Schneiderlein, „da thäte man wohl ein übriges, aber die Kirschen hängen mir zu hoch:
sentences.l: “The reward is certainly great,” thought the little tailor, “for that one would indeed do something extra, but the cherries hang too high for me:
sentences.i: “The reward is great enough, to be sure,” thought the little tailor, “one would go to some trouble for that — but the cherries hang too high for me:
sentences.n: ein übriges thun is to do more than is required. thäte is the past subjunctive of thun (modern tun), “would do.” The cherries out of reach are proverbial for what is not to be had, and mir is the dative of the person concerned.

sentences.t: wenn ich danach steige, so bricht unter mir der Ast, und ich falle herab.“
sentences.l: if I climb after them, then the branch breaks under me, and I fall down.”
sentences.i: if I climb after them, the branch will break under me and I shall fall.”
sentences.n: danach steigen is to climb up after them. The present tense stands for the future, as German regularly lets it; herabfallen is separable: falle … herab.

sentences.t: Er gieng nach Haus, setzte sich mit unterschlagenen Beinen auf seinen Arbeitstisch und bedachte sich was zu thun wäre.
sentences.l: He went home, set himself with crossed legs on his work table and considered what was to be done.
sentences.i: He went home, sat down cross-legged on his work table and considered what was to be done.
sentences.n: mit unterschlagenen Beinen is the tailor’s cross-legged sitting on his bench, the trade’s own posture — the picture the modern word Schneidersitz still keeps. was zu thun wäre is the subjunctive of a deliberating question.

sentences.t: „Es geht nicht,“ rief er endlich aus, „ich will fort, hier kann ich doch nicht in Ruhe leben.“
sentences.l: “It does not go,” he cried out at last, “I will away, here I cannot live in peace after all.”
sentences.i: “It cannot be done,” he cried out at last; “I will be off — here I cannot live in peace.”
sentences.n: ausrufen is separable: rief … aus. ich will fort has no verb of motion at all — “I want [to be] away” — and German simply leaves it out.

sentences.t: Er schnürte sein Bündel und eilte zum Thore hinaus.
sentences.l: He laced up his bundle and hurried out of the gate.
sentences.n: Almost word for word the sentence used at his last flight from the city; the tale repeats it to mark the pattern.

sentences.t: Als er auf die Wiesen kam, erblickte er seinen alten Freund, den Storch, der da, wie ein Weltweiser, auf und abgieng, zuweilen still stand, einen Frosch in nähere Betrachtung nahm und ihn endlich verschluckte.
sentences.l: When he came to the meadows, he caught sight of his old friend the stork, who was going up and down there like a world-sage, stood still now and then, took a frog into closer consideration and finally swallowed it.
sentences.i: When he came to the meadows he caught sight of his old friend the stork, who was pacing up and down there like a philosopher, standing still now and then, taking a frog into closer consideration and at last swallowing it.
sentences.n: ein Weltweiser is the old German word for a philosopher, literally a world-wise man. in nähere Betrachtung nehmen is deliberately grand language for a bird eating a frog, and the joke is the tale’s own. The 1857 text writes auf und abgieng with the second half joined.

sentences.t: Der Storch kam heran und begrüßte ihn.
sentences.l: The stork came up and greeted him.
sentences.n: herankommen is separable: kam … heran.

sentences.t: „Ich sehe,“ hub er an, „du hast deinen Ranzen auf dem Rücken, warum willst du die Stadt verlassen?“
sentences.l: “I see,” he began, “you have your pack on your back, why do you want to leave the city?”
sentences.i: “I see,” he began, “you have your pack on your back — why do you want to leave the city?”
sentences.n: hub … an is the old past of anheben, to begin to speak, where modern German would say fing an. Ein Ranzen is a pack carried on the back.

sentences.t: Der Schneider erzählte ihm was der König von ihm verlangt hatte und er nicht erfüllen konnte, und jammerte über sein Misgeschick.
sentences.l: The tailor told him what the king had demanded of him and he could not fulfil, and lamented over his mishap.
sentences.i: The tailor told him what the king had demanded of him and he could not perform, and lamented his mishap.
sentences.n: Misgeschick is the 1857 spelling of Missgeschick, ill luck. The second clause hangs on the same was: what the king demanded and what he could not fulfil.

sentences.t: „Laß dir darüber keine grauen Haare wachsen,“ sagte der Storch, „ich will dir aus der Noth helfen.
sentences.l: “Do not let any grey hairs grow on you over it,” said the stork, “I will help you out of the trouble.
sentences.i: “Do not let it give you grey hairs,” said the stork, “I will help you out of your trouble.
sentences.n: sich keine grauen Haare wachsen lassen is the fixed idiom for not fretting, with the dative dir as the person it happens to. Noth is the 1857 spelling of Not.

sentences.t: Schon lange bringe ich die Wickelkinder in die Stadt, da kann ich auch einmal einen kleinen Prinzen aus dem Brunnen holen.
sentences.l: For a long time now I bring the swaddled children into the city, so I can fetch a little prince out of the well for once too.
sentences.i: I have been bringing babies in swaddling clothes to the city this long while, so I can fetch a little prince out of the well for once as well.
sentences.n: German uses the present with schon lange where English needs a perfect: “I have long been bringing.” Wickelkinder are infants in swaddling bands; the stork brings the babies, and in the older telling he fetches them out of a well or pond.

sentences.t: Geh heim und verhalte dich ruhig.
sentences.l: Go home and conduct yourself quietly.
sentences.i: Go home and keep quiet.
sentences.n: sich verhalten is reflexive, “to conduct oneself”; both verbs here are imperatives.

sentences.t: Heut über neun Tage begib dich in das königliche Schloß, da will ich kommen.“
sentences.l: Nine days from today betake yourself to the royal castle, there I will come.”
sentences.i: Nine days from today betake yourself to the royal castle, and I will come there.”
sentences.n: heut über neun Tage is the old way of counting forward — “this day nine days.” begib is the imperative of sich begeben, with the e → i vowel change that strong verbs make in the singular imperative.

sentences.t: Das Schneiderlein gieng nach Haus und war zu rechter Zeit in dem Schloß.
sentences.l: The little tailor went home and was in the castle at the right time.
sentences.n: zu rechter Zeit, with no article, is “in good time, punctually.”

sentences.t: Nicht lange, so kam der Storch heran geflogen und klopfte ans Fenster.
sentences.l: Not long, and the stork came flying up and knocked at the window.
sentences.i: It was not long before the stork came flying up and knocked at the window.
sentences.n: Nicht lange, so … is an elliptical “before long,” with no verb at all in the first half. kam … geflogen is again kommen with a participle.

sentences.t: Der Schneider öffnete ihm, und Vetter Langbein stieg vorsichtig herein und gieng mit gravitätischen Schritten über den glatten Marmorboden;
sentences.l: The tailor opened to him, and Cousin Longleg stepped carefully in and walked with grave strides over the smooth marble floor;
sentences.i: The tailor opened to him, and Cousin Longleg stepped carefully in and walked with solemn strides across the smooth marble floor;
sentences.n: öffnete ihm — “opened to him,” with the person in the dative and no object expressed at all. gravitätisch is a Latinate word for a stately, weighty bearing, and it is chosen for the comedy of it.

sentences.t: er hatte aber ein Kind im Schnabel, das schön wie ein Engel, und seine Händchen nach der Königin ausstreckte.
sentences.l: but he had a child in his beak, that [was] beautiful as an angel, and stretched out its little hands toward the queen.
sentences.i: but he had a child in his beak, one that was beautiful as an angel and stretched out its little hands toward the queen.
sentences.n: The verb of the first relative clause is left out — das schön wie ein Engel [war] — and the literal supplies it in square brackets, since English cannot leave it standing; the brackets are ours, not the Grimms’. Händchen is the diminutive of Hand, and ausstrecken is separable: streckte … aus.

sentences.t: Er legte es ihr auf den Schoß, und sie herzte und küßte es, und war vor Freude außer sich.
sentences.l: He laid it on her lap, and she hugged and kissed it, and was beside herself for joy.
sentences.i: He laid it in her lap, and she hugged and kissed it, and was beside herself with joy.
sentences.n: ihr auf den Schoß is the dative of the person and the accusative of the place the child comes to rest in. herzen is to press to the heart, from Herz.

sentences.t: Der Storch nahm, bevor er wieder wegflog, seine Reisetasche von der Schulter herab und überreichte sie der Königin.
sentences.l: The stork took, before he flew away again, his travelling bag down from his shoulder and handed it over to the queen.
sentences.i: Before he flew off again, the stork took his travelling bag down from his shoulder and presented it to the queen.
sentences.n: German can push a whole clause in between the verb and its object, as here between nahm and seine Reisetasche; English cannot, and the idiomatic line moves it to the front. herabnehmen is separable.

sentences.t: Es steckten Düten darin mit bunten Zuckererbsen, sie wurden unter die kleinen Prinzessinnen vertheilt.
sentences.l: There were stuck in it paper cones with coloured sugar peas; they were shared out among the little princesses.
sentences.i: In it were paper cones of coloured sugar peas, and these were shared out among the little princesses.
sentences.n: Es steckten is again the placeholder es with the real subject following the verb. Eine Düte (modern Tüte) is a twist of paper for sweets, and Zuckererbsen are little round sugar sweets. vertheilt is the 1857 spelling of verteilt.

sentences.t: Die älteste aber erhielt nichts, sondern bekam den lustigen Schneider zum Mann.
sentences.l: The eldest, however, received nothing, but got the merry tailor for a husband.
sentences.i: But the eldest received nothing — she got the merry tailor for a husband instead.
sentences.n: erhielt and bekam are both “received,” set side by side so that the second lands as the joke. zum Mann, like zur Frau earlier, is the marriage phrase.

sentences.t: „Es ist mir geradeso,“ sprach der Schneider, „als wenn ich das große Loos gewonnen hätte.
sentences.l: “It is to me just so,” said the tailor, “as if I had won the great lot.
sentences.i: “I feel just as if I had won the great prize in the lottery,” said the tailor.
sentences.n: es ist mir, als wenn … is the set way of saying how something feels, with the person in the dative. Loos is the 1857 spelling of Los, a lottery ticket, and das große Loos is the top prize; hätte is subjunctive after als wenn, marking the comparison as unreal.

sentences.t: Meine Mutter hatte doch recht, die sagte immer, wer auf Gott vertraut und nur Glück hat, dem kanns nicht fehlen.“
sentences.l: My mother was right after all, she always said, whoever trusts in God and only has luck, to him it cannot fail.”
sentences.i: My mother was right after all — she always said that whoever trusts in God and has luck besides cannot go wrong.”
sentences.n: die picks up Meine Mutter as a demonstrative, common in speech. wer …, dem … is the correlative pair, “whoever …, to him …,” and kanns is kann es. The mother’s saying quietly puts luck beside trust in God, which is the tale’s own verdict on the tailor.

sentences.t: Der Schuster mußte die Schuhe machen, in welchen das Schneiderlein auf dem Hochzeitfest tanzte, hernach ward ihm befohlen die Stadt auf immer zu verlassen.
sentences.l: The cobbler had to make the shoes in which the little tailor danced at the wedding feast; afterwards it was commanded him to leave the city for ever.
sentences.i: The cobbler had to make the shoes the little tailor danced in at the wedding feast, and afterwards he was ordered to leave the city for good.
sentences.n: ward is again the old past of werden, here building a passive: ward ihm befohlen, “it was commanded to him.” befehlen puts the person in the dative, so German cannot say “he was ordered” as English does. hernach is “afterwards.”

sentences.t: Der Weg nach dem Wald führte ihn zu dem Galgen.
sentences.l: The way to the forest led him to the gallows.
sentences.n: The tale brings him back to the exact spot where he blinded the tailor and left him lying; nothing is said about that, and nothing needs to be.

sentences.t: Von Zorn, Wuth und der Hitze des Tages ermüdet, warf er sich nieder.
sentences.l: Wearied by anger, rage and the heat of the day, he threw himself down.
sentences.i: Worn out with anger, rage and the heat of the day, he threw himself down.
sentences.n: Zorn and Wuth (modern Wut) are piled up as near-synonyms, anger and fury. The participle phrase stands in front of the main clause, exactly as English allows.

sentences.t: Als er die Augen zumachte und schlafen wollte, stürzten die beiden Krähen von den Köpfen der Gehenkten mit lautem Geschrei herab und hackten ihm die Augen aus.
sentences.l: When he shut his eyes and wanted to sleep, the two crows plunged down from the heads of the hanged men with loud screaming and hacked his eyes out.
sentences.i: When he shut his eyes and would have slept, the two crows plunged down from the heads of the hanged men with loud screaming and hacked his eyes out.
sentences.n: zumachen, herabstürzen and aushacken are all separable. der Gehenkten is the genitive plural of the participle used as a noun. These are the same two crows that sat on those heads while the tailor got his eyes back; the tale answers the deed exactly and says nothing more about it.

sentences.t: Unsinnig rannte er in den Wald und muß darin verschmachtet sein, denn es hat ihn niemand wieder gesehen oder etwas von ihm gehört.
sentences.l: Out of his senses he ran into the forest and must have wasted away in it, for nobody has seen him again or heard anything of him.
sentences.i: Out of his senses he ran into the forest, and must have perished there, for nobody has seen him again or heard anything of him.
sentences.n: unsinnig is “out of one’s wits,” not the modern “nonsensical.” muß … verschmachtet sein is inference, “must have,” and verschmachten is the very word the blinded tailor used of himself in this forest. The tale closes with no word of judgment, on a report that nobody knows.

glossary.ansehen: ansehen — to look at (infinitive); as a noun das Ansehen, standing, repute
glossary.backen: die Backe — cheeks (pl.; not the verb backen, to bake)
glossary.band: binden — to bind, tie (3rd sg. past; here zusammenbinden, particle at the end); also das Band, a band
glossary.blitz: der Blitz — lightning (schnell wie der Blitz: quick as lightning)
glossary.breite: ausbreiten — to spread out (imperative sg.; the particle follows: breite … aus); also die Breite, breadth
glossary.drückt: drücken — to press, to weigh on (3rd sg. present; mich drückt etwas: something weighs on me)
glossary.erhalten: erhalten — to keep, preserve (infinitive; also as past participle, received)
glossary.füllen: das Füllen — the foal, colt (noun; not the verb füllen, to fill)
glossary.gefangene: der Gefangene — the captive (adjective used as a noun; also feminine, die Gefangene)
glossary.gesicht: das Gesicht — face; in older use also the eyesight
glossary.graben: graben — to dig (infinitive); also der Graben, a ditch
glossary.heiliger: heilig — holy (masc. nom. sg.); also der Heilige, a saint
glossary.hieb: der Hieb — a stroke, a blow (with a switch or a blade); also hieb, hewed, the past of hauen
glossary.kehre: sich an etwas kehren — to pay heed to a thing (1st sg. present; also kehren, to sweep, to turn)
glossary.kehrte: umkehren — turned back, turned about (3rd sg. past; separable um-, the particle follows)
glossary.knöpfe: der Knopf — knob, ball (plural; on a spire, the gilded ball under the cross); also a button
glossary.krähen: die Krähe — crow (plural); also krähen, to crow
glossary.lasse: lassen — to let (3rd sg. subjunctive I of reported speech; also 1st sg. present)
glossary.lauf: laufen — to run (imperative sg.); also der Lauf, running, course (in vollem Lauf: at full speed)
glossary.leichter: leicht — light in weight (masc. nom. sg.); also as a comparative adverb, more easily
glossary.leid: das Leid — harm, sorrow (ein Leid zufügen: to do harm); also leid in es thut mir leid, I am sorry
glossary.muth: der Muth — courage, heart (1857 spelling of Mut; den Muth verlieren, to lose heart)
glossary.naht: die Naht — the seam (here the noun, not the verb nahen, to draw near)
glossary.nest: das Nest — nest; dismissively, a tiny out-of-the-way town
glossary.nähe: nähen — to sew (imperative sg.); also die Nähe, nearness
glossary.richtet: richten — to judge, to sit in judgment (3rd sg. present)
glossary.schlag: schlagen — to strike, hammer (imperative); also der Schlag, a blow
glossary.schoß: der Schoß — lap; also schoß, shot, the past of schießen
glossary.sei: sein — be (imperative sg.); also 3rd sg. subjunctive I in reported speech
glossary.sonst: sonst — otherwise, else; also formerly, in earlier days
glossary.stich: der Stich — stitch of a needle; also a prick or stab
glossary.streich: streichen — to spread, smear (imperative); also der Streich, a trick or prank
glossary.stößt: stoßen — to strike, thrust (3rd sg. present; of a hawk, to swoop on its prey)
glossary.unsinnig: unsinnig — out of one’s wits, frantic (not the modern sense, nonsensical)
glossary.unterschied: unterscheiden — to make out, distinguish (3rd sg. past); also der Unterschied, difference
glossary.vertheilt: vertheilen — to share out, distribute (past participle; 1857 spelling of verteilen)
glossary.vertraut: vertrauen — to trust (3rd sg. present; auf Gott vertrauen, to trust in God); also vertraut, familiar
glossary.volk: das Volk — people, folk; of bees, the colony of a hive
glossary.wache: wachen — to be awake, to keep watch (1st sg. present; not die Wache, a guard)
glossary.weg: der Weg — way, road (also weg, away, as a separable prefix)
glossary.weiß: wissen — to know (1st and 3rd sg. present); also weiß, white (adj.)
glossary.zieh: abziehen — to be off, clear off (imperative sg.; the particle follows: zieh … ab); also ziehen, to pull
glossary.ärger: arg — bad (comparative: worse, more outrageous); also der Ärger, vexation
